verification_levels.verified-web: checked against accessible primary/reputable secondary sources (2026-08-24)
verification_levels.verified-primary: checked against full judgment/statute text with paragraph pin cite (target state)

sub_tests.test: Opinion or intention is not actionable UNLESS not honestly held (state of mind is itself a fact), or the opinion is given by a party with superior knowledge so as to imply facts justifying it; pure opinion where both parties know there is no factual basis is not actionable.

auth.case: Smith v Land and House Property Corp

sub_tests.test: A literally true but misleading partial statement is a misrepresentation.
A statement true when made but falsified by a change of circumstances before contracting must be corrected; silence is then actionable.
Conduct can constitute a representation (including participation with undisclosed knowledge); mere silence generally cannot — there is no general duty of disclosure.

auth.case: Spice Girls Ltd v Aprilia World Service

sub_tests.test: The representation must be addressed to the claimant or intended to reach them; a prospectus is exhausted on the original allottees and does not extend to market purchasers.
The representee must have been aware of the representation; a concealment never seen cannot have operated on the mind.
The representation must be a real and substantial cause of entering the contract; it need not be the sole inducement.

A material representation calculated to induce raises an inference/presumption of inducement; in fraud the presumption is very difficult to rebut and the test is whether the representation was 'a' cause, not 'the' cause. Jurisdictions diverge — see timeline T2.

auth.case: BV Nederlandse Industrie van Eiprodukten v Rembrandt Enterprises

sub_tests.test: Belief in the truth of the statement is not required: reliance survives suspicion of falsity where the statement materially influenced the decision (settlement context).
An opportunity to discover the truth is no defence; sole reliance on the representee's own independent investigation is.
Knowingly false, without belief in its truth, or reckless whether true or false (Lord Herschell). An honest but negligent belief is insufficient — 'ought to have known' does not establish fraud.
No proof of fraud needed; the burden is REVERSED — the representor must prove objectively reasonable ground to believe AND actual belief up to the time of contract (majority; Denning MR dissenting).

auth.case: Howard Marine v A Ogden & Sons

sub_tests.test: Rescission is available for all variants subject to bars: affirmation after knowledge, lapse of time, impossibility of restitution, third-party rights.
All loss directly flowing from the fraud, not limited by foreseeability; the date-of-transaction rule is applied flexibly where the fraud continues to operate.

auth.case: Smith New Court v Scrimgeour Vickers

sub_tests.test: s.2(1)-type damages assessed on the deceit measure via the 'fiction of fraud' — formally good law in England but doubted (left open in Smith New Court); ADOPTED and undoubted in Hong Kong since 1991; open in Singapore with SGCA obiter against.

auth.note: criticised; correctness left open in Smith New Court

auth.case: Long Year Development v Tse Fuk Man Norman
auth.source: quoted verbatim in Wong Yuk Lan v Car's City [2024] HKDC 804 at [90] and pin-cited in Joytex [2018] HKCFI 2286 at §142 and Alireza v Elman [2026] HKCFI 4060 at [199]
auth.note: DHCJ Andrew Li QC (later CJ): 'the measure of damages for s 3(1) of the Ordinance is the same as that for deceit' — Royscot followed as 'highly persuasive as the legislative provisions are identical'
applies the deceit measure under Cap. 284 s.3(1) as ratio; DHCJ Alexander Stock SC

auth.case: Wong Yuk Lan v Car's City Co Ltd
auth.note: quotes Long Year at 407D-408D in full; awards s.3(1) damages on the tortious/deceit measure

defences.test: Contractual estoppel: parties may agree that no representations were made or relied on, barring non-fraudulent claims. Exceptions: fraud can never be excluded; statutory reasonableness control applies where the jurisdiction provides it. Sharpest cross-jurisdiction divergence — see timeline T1.

auth.case: Springwell Navigation v JP Morgan Chase

defences.test: The representee relied solely on their own independent investigation rather than the statement.

sections.s.3: exclusion clauses subject to UCTA 1977 s.11(1) reasonableness (as substituted; consumer contracts carved out by CRA 2015)

HK.name: Hong Kong SAR
HK.regime: misrepresentation remedial statute + common law (mirrors England)
HK.apex: Court of Final Appeal (Basic Law art. 82)
HK.authority_rule: Pre-1997 Privy Council decisions on HK appeals bind below CFA; pre-1997 House of Lords persuasive (great weight); post-1997 English and all overseas persuasive only (Basic Law arts. 8, 84; A Solicitor v Law Society of Hong Kong (2008) 11 HKCFAR 117)

sections.s.4: exclusion clauses of no effect unless reasonable per Control of Exemption Clauses Ordinance (Cap. 71) s.3(1)

statutes.source: mirror + CFA quotation in Green Park; official e-Legislation text not fetched

cases.name: Green Park Properties Ltd v Dorku Ltd
cases.holding: Misrepresentation about a rear yard in a property sale induced the purchase; rescission plus expenses. The entire agreement clause was of no effect under MO s.4 for failing CECO s.3(1) reasonableness.

cases.name: DBS Bank (HK) v San-Hot HK Industrial
cases.holding: Contractual estoppel following Peekay/Springwell 'also applies in Hong Kong'; non-reliance terms defeated mis-selling claims.
cases.note: [2013] 4 HKC 1 parallel citation and the SFO s.108 analysis at §16 per DHCJ Pow SC confirmed from Li Yuhong v OOO Securities [2025] HKCFI 5270 at [111]

cases.name: DBS Bank (HK) v Sit Pan Jit
cases.holding: Non-reliance clauses upheld via contractual estoppel, extending to statutory claims under SFO s.108.

cases.name: Chang Pui Yin v Bank of Singapore
cases.holding: Counter-limit: non-reliance and non-advisory clauses unenforceable on the facts as unconscionable and as unreasonable exclusions under CECO, for unsophisticated customers.

cases.name: Shine Grace Investment v Citibank NA
cases.holding: No inducement where the claimant's principal was an experienced independent trader who would have traded anyway.
cases.pin: HCCL 28/2008, judgment of Ng J dated 30 July 2018 (corrigenda 7 August 2018)
cases.note: date corrected: HKLII metadata records 29 July 2018, the judgment itself is dated 30 July 2018

cases.name: Long Year Development Ltd v Tse Fuk Man Norman
cases.holding: The measure of damages under Cap. 284 s.3(1) is the same as for deceit. Royscot followed within months of it being decided, on the express ground that it was 'highly persuasive as the legislative provisions are identical'. But the deceit measure is the TORTIOUS measure: the plaintiff is put in the position he would have been in had the representation not been made, not the position had it been true. Loss-of-a-chance claim on a putative alternative purchase rejected for want of evidence (409F-410D).
cases.note: DHCJ Andrew Li QC, later the first Chief Justice of the CFA. Judgment text not on HKLII (pre-1997); verified from verbatim quotation in Wong Yuk Lan [2024] HKDC 804 at [90] plus pin cites in Joytex [2018] HKCFI 2286 §142 and Alireza [2026] HKCFI 4060 [199]

cases.name: Joytex Development Ltd v Super Homes Ltd
cases.holding: s.3(1) damages awarded on the deceit measure; damages under s.3(1) may be claimed together with rescission. Objective construction of representations from the perspective of a reasonable person in the representee's position, taking the representee's sophistication into account (§77(2)); cumulative effect of multiple representations (§80); no defence that the representee could have discovered the truth (§116).

cases.name: Ng Lai Ling Winnie v Ng Yuk Pui Kelly
cases.holding: Contractual estoppel arises ONLY between parties to a contract and only on the basis of their mutual agreement, and only so far as concerns those aspects of their relationship to which the agreement was directed. A stranger to the contract containing the acknowledgment cannot raise it; as against him the transaction is res inter alios acta. Peekay treated as 'the leading case'; First Tower Trustees quoted.
cases.note: Ribeiro PJ, Fok PJ, Chan NPJ; reasons given on refusing leave to appeal. A reasoned Appeal Committee determination, NOT a substantive CFA appeal judgment — persuasive at apex level but it does not settle contractual estoppel in the mis-selling context

cases.name: Li Yuhong v OOO Securities (HK) Group Ltd
cases.holding: Consolidated statement of the HK misrepresentation elements. Adopts Hayward v Zurich §§33-35 on inducement (need not be the sole inducement; presumption on proof of falsity plus entry, strongest in fraud) and restates the Cap. 284 s.3(1) deceit measure.

cases.name: Koo Ming Kown v The Baptist Convention of Hong Kong
cases.holding: The inducement 'presumption' is an inference of FACT, not a presumption of law, and is rebuttable on all the relevant evidence including the claimant's own testimony (Zurich [34]; BV Nederlandse [2020] QB 551 at [25], [32] per Longmore LJ). Appeal on inducement dismissed.
cases.note: Au, Chow and Anthony Chan JJA; judgment of the Court by Anthony Chan JA. Places the HK CA alongside SGCA (Wee Chiaw Sek Anna) and against the stronger English reading — and against the HK CFI's own restatement in Li Yuhong [2025] HKCFI 5270 [109] months earlier

cases.name: Alireza v Elman
cases.holding: Obiter: a claimant pleading the CONTRACTUAL measure ('as if the representations had been true') for a s.3(1)/tortious misrepresentation claim fails to prove damage; the tortious counterfactual must be pleaded and evidenced.
cases.note: misrepresentation claim not engaged on the findings; observations expressly made only 'if necessary'

gaps: D1: no SUBSTANTIVE CFA appeal judgment on contractual estoppel. The apex has spoken only through a reasoned Appeal Committee determination refusing leave (Ng Lai Ling Winnie [2021] HKCFA 40 at [24]-[27]), which confines the doctrine to the contracting parties but does not address non-reliance clauses in the mis-selling setting; adoption there still rests at CFI (San-Hot, Sit Pan Jit) with CA-level qualification (Chang Pui Yin).

E3c: HK is internally inconsistent — the CA reads the inducement presumption as an inference of fact (Koo Ming Kown [2026] HKCA 372 [67]) while the CFI had restated the stronger English version months earlier (Li Yuhong [2025] HKCFI 5270 [109]). Unresolved above CA level.

E5c: the HK line adopting Royscot has never been tested above first instance. Long Year (1991), Joytex (2018) and Alireza (2026) are all CFI/HC; Wong Yuk Lan (2024) is DC. No CA or CFA ruling on the Cap. 284 s.3(1) measure was located.

SG.name: Singapore
SG.regime: received remedial statute + received common law (AELA 1993)
SG.authority_rule: English precedent persuasive only; Practice Statement (Judicial Precedent) [1994] — SGCA departs where adherence causes injustice or constrains development

sections.s.2(1): damages, reversed burden (same structure as UK)
sections.s.4: SG-only transitional: no application before 12 Nov 1993

sections.s.3: English common law continues as at 12.11.1993 so far as applicable to the circumstances of Singapore
sections.First Sched Pt II item 9: UCTA Part I (except ss.1(1)(c), 1(3)(b)) and Part III

cases.name: Panatron v Lee Cheow Lee
cases.holding: Deceit elements per Derry v Peek; inducement requires a 'real and substantial part', not sole causation; failure to verify is no defence.

cases.name: Tan Chin Seng v Raffles Town Club (No 2)
cases.holding: A statement of intention is actionable only if the intention is not honestly held.

cases.name: Orient Centre Investments v Societe Generale
cases.holding: Non-reliance and acknowledgment clauses defeated misrepresentation claims between sophisticated parties.

cases.name: Als Memasa v UBS AG
cases.holding: Obiter: courts may need to reconsider full immunity via non-reliance clauses for unsophisticated customers; UCTA applicability expressly left open.

cases.name: Wee Chiaw Sek Anna v Ng Li-Ann Genevieve
cases.holding: The inducement 'presumption' is a fair inference of fact, not of law; the burden of proving reliance stays on the representee — weaker than the English articulation.

cases.name: RBC Properties v Defu Furniture
cases.holding: s.2(1) imposes a dual burden (objective reasonable ground plus subjective belief to contract time), demanding and fact-centric; Royscot's fiction of fraud doubted obiter and left open.

divergences: Inducement presumption downgraded to an inference of fact (Wee Chiaw Sek Anna)
s.2(1) measure: Royscot not adopted; SGCA lean is the negligence measure (RBC, obiter)
s.3 references the pre-2015 UCTA text — no CRA 2015 consumer carve-out

AU.name: Australia
AU.regime: conduct prohibition, no fault (sui generis) + retained common law deceit/rescission
AU.apex: High Court of Australia (PC appeals ended: 1968/1975 Acts; Australia Acts 1986)
AU.authority_rule: English precedent persuasive only — Cook v Cook (1986) 162 CLR 376, 390 (dictum standard; case overruled on substance by Imbree v McNeilly [2008] HCA 40)

statutes.ref: Australian Consumer Law s.18 (Sch 2, Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth)); successor of TPA 1974 s.52

sections.text: A person must not, in trade or commerce, engage in conduct that is misleading or deceptive or is likely to mislead or deceive
sections.scope gate: in trade or commerce (Concrete Constructions v Nelson (1990) 169 CLR 594)
sections.remedies: s.236 damages (6yr), s.237 compensation orders, s.243 order menu incl. void ab initio, s.232 injunctions
sections.exclusion by contract: NOT PERMITTED (Henjo Investments (1988) 39 FCR 546; Clark Equipment (1987) 71 ALR 367)
sections.non-reliance clauses: relevant to causation only (Campbell v Backoffice [2009] HCA 25, French CJ at [31])

acl_s18_elements: misleading or deceptive or likely to mislead (objective; ordinary-reasonable-member test for mass conduct — Campomar v Nike [2000] HCA 12; whole-context assessment for identified persons — Butcher v Lachlan Elder [2004] HCA 60; conduit principle — Google v ACCC [2013] HCA 1)
for damages: loss 'because of' the conduct — reliance is the usual causal route; 'a' cause suffices

cases.name: Henjo Investments v Collins Marrickville
cases.holding: Silence and half-truths can mislead; contractual disclaimers cannot shield s.52 (now s.18) liability.

cases.name: Butcher v Lachlan Elder Realty
cases.holding: An agent passing on vendor-sourced information without adopting it, with disclaimers in context, did not engage in misleading conduct.

cases.name: Campbell v Backoffice Investments
cases.holding: A contractual disclaimer of reliance ordinarily bears on causation and will not necessarily break the causal link.

cases.name: Google Inc v ACCC
cases.holding: Conduit principle: an intermediary merely displaying advertisers' representations does not adopt them.

cases.name: Magill v Magill
cases.holding: Retained common-law deceit follows Derry v Peek — the English backbone applies to the deceit claim.

T1.title_en: Effect of non-reliance / entire agreement clauses
